answer.rationale: The primary contract expires in 14 days with no auto-renew, and finance demands an 18% cost cut. Switching vendors (memory_c2 precedent) could cut unit cost but introduces delivery risk at a moment when the assembly line is at 94% committed volume with zero buffer—unacceptable given the primary objective explicitly forbids increasing delivery risk. Adding a second source (memory_c3) is valuable for resilience but does not directly address the 18% cut mandate and consumes the single decision slot without resolving the imminent expiry. Deferring (memory_c5) is not viable because the contract lapses in 14 days; there is nothing non-critical to defer. Renewing outright (memory_c1) preserves continuity but leaves cost untouched, failing the finance mandate. That leaves negotiation at renewal (memory_c4) combined with the multi-year volume-pricing lever (memory_c6): renegotiating with the incumbent on price, payment terms, and a multi-year commitment can simultaneously deliver the required cost reduction and lock in uninterrupted supply. I verify memory_c6 to confirm the volume-pricing mechanism and its cost-reduction magnitude, and memory_c4 to confirm the renegotiation playbook and achievable margin recovery. If both archives support a combined saving approaching 18%, I execute negotiate_terms with the incumbent before the 14-day expiry. If the combined saving falls materially short, I would need to revisit switch_primary_vendor in the next cycle, accepting onboarding risk then rather than compounding it now under time pressure.
